title: Transistor switching and logic families (RTL, DTL, TTL, CMOS)
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE TRANSISTOR
SECTION 5.3. TRANSISTOR SWITCHING AND LOGIC FAMILIES (RTL, DTL, TTL, CMOS)

A transistor is a switch; a computer needs millions or billions of switches wired into gates that can drive one another reliably. Between the 1950s and the 1980s engineers developed a series of standard circuit styles, called logic families, for building gates from transistors. Each family traded off speed, power, noise tolerance and cost differently, and each was suited to the manufacturing technology of its time. This section walks through the main families, ending with CMOS, the technology of essentially every processor and AI accelerator made today. You will meet several of these families in lab work, datasheets and old equipment.

1. What makes a good logic gate?

For gates to be connected in long chains, the circuit must satisfy several engineering requirements:

  - Level restoration: a slightly degraded input (say 4.2 V instead of 5 V for a "1") must produce a clean full-level output, so noise does not accumulate through stages. This requires gain greater than 1 around the switching threshold.
  - Noise margins: the range of input voltage that is still read correctly. For a family with guaranteed output levels VOH (high) and VOL (low) and input thresholds VIH and VIL:

        NMH = VOH - VIH       (noise margin, high)
        NML = VIL - VOL       (noise margin, low)

  - Fan-out: the number of gate inputs one output can drive while still meeting its levels.
  - Propagation delay: time from an input change to the output change, typically measured at 50 percent points.
  - Power dissipation, both static (while not switching) and dynamic (when switching).

A useful figure of merit is the speed-power product (delay multiplied by power, in joules), which measures energy per switching operation. It has fallen by many orders of magnitude from the 1960s to today, which is the real engine of the computing revolution.

2. RTL: resistor-transistor logic

The simplest family uses the common-emitter inverter of Section 5.2. For a NOR gate: connect several input resistors to the bases of several transistors whose collectors share a single pull-up resistor Rc to Vcc.

    Vcc
     |
     Rc
     |-------- output
     |      |
    Q1 C   Q2 C
    B|      B|
    Rb      Rb
    |        |
    A        B
    (emitters to ground)

If either input is high, its transistor saturates and pulls the output low. Output high only if both inputs are low:

    Out = NOT (A OR B)

RTL was used in early integrated circuits. Fairchild's Micrologic RTL chips were among the first commercial ICs, and the Apollo Guidance Computer, which flew the Apollo missions to the Moon, was built almost entirely from RTL NOR gates: about 4,100 single three-input NOR gate chips in Block I and about 2,800 chips, mostly dual three-input NOR gates, in Block II. Choosing one universal gate type (recall from Section 1.1 that NOR alone can build any function) simplified qualification and manufacturing.

Weaknesses: low noise margins, limited fan-out, and slowness because of saturation and the resistive pull-up charging load capacitance.

3. DTL: diode-transistor logic

DTL performs the logic with diodes (diode AND, as in Section 4.1) and uses a transistor inverter for gain and inversion, giving a NAND gate:

  - Inputs connect through diodes to a node pulled up by a resistor. If any input is low, the node is pulled low (diode AND).
  - The node drives the transistor base through level-shifting diodes. If the node is high (all inputs high), the transistor saturates and the output goes low.

    Out = NOT (A AND B)

DTL had better noise margins and fan-out than RTL and was popular in the early 1960s.

4. TTL: transistor-transistor logic

TTL replaced DTL's input diodes with a single multi-emitter transistor, a device that is easy to make in integrated form. The circuit, first described by James Buie at TRW in the early 1960s and introduced as integrated circuits by Sylvania in 1963, was standardized and popularized by Texas Instruments with the 5400 series (military temperature range) in 1964 and the 7400 series in 1966. The 7400 family became the standard building block of digital electronics for about two decades; the part number "7400" itself is a quad 2-input NAND gate.

The standard TTL NAND gate has three stages:

  1. Input: a multi-emitter transistor. If any emitter is low, it pulls current out of the base of the next stage, turning it off.
  2. Phase splitter: a transistor that produces complementary signals to drive the output stage.
  3. Totem-pole output: two transistors stacked, one actively pulling up toward Vcc and one pulling down to ground. Only one is on at a time (ideally).

Active pull-up and pull-down allow the gate to charge and discharge load capacitance quickly in both directions, much faster than a resistor pull-up.

Standard TTL parameters (nominal, 5 V supply):

    VOH min 2.4 V, VIH min 2.0 V  -> NMH = 0.4 V
    VOL max 0.4 V, VIL max 0.8 V  -> NML = 0.4 V
    fan-out 10 standard loads
    propagation delay about 10 ns
    power about 10 mW per gate

Variants improved the trade-offs: Schottky TTL (74S) and low-power Schottky (74LS) used Schottky diodes to prevent deep saturation (Section 5.2), cutting storage delay; later "advanced" families went further. A note for practical work: TTL inputs that are left floating tend to read as high, but unconnected inputs pick up noise, so tie unused inputs to a defined level.

5. ECL: emitter-coupled logic

For maximum speed, ECL never lets its transistors saturate. Its core is a differential pair: two transistors share a common emitter current source; whichever has the higher base voltage takes almost all the current. A difference of a few hundred millivolts steers the current from one side to the other. Outputs are taken through emitter followers.

Because there is no saturation and voltage swings are small (about 0.8 V), ECL is very fast, but it draws constant current whether switching or not, so it is power-hungry. ECL was used in the fastest mainframes and supercomputers of the 1960s to 1980s, including Seymour Cray's machines. It provides complementary outputs (OR and NOR) for free.

6. The MOSFET

The field-effect transistor that Bell Labs could not make in 1945 (Section 5.2) was finally achieved in 1959 by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs. Atalla's key contribution was surface passivation: growing a thin layer of silicon dioxide on silicon by thermal oxidation, which neutralized the troublesome surface states.

Structure of an n-channel MOSFET (NMOS): a p-type silicon substrate with two heavily doped n-type regions, the source and drain. Between them, on top of the silicon, a thin insulating oxide layer, and on top of that a conducting gate (originally aluminum, later polysilicon, now metal again in advanced processes).

Operation:

  - With gate voltage Vgs below a threshold Vt, the region between source and drain is p-type, so there are two back-to-back p-n junctions and no current flows. Off.
  - With Vgs above Vt, the positive gate attracts electrons to the surface, forming a thin n-type "inversion layer" channel connecting source and drain. Current flows. On.

The gate is insulated by the oxide, so in steady state it draws essentially no current, like the grid of a vacuum tube, only better.

The classic "square-law" model (long-channel):

    Cutoff (Vgs < Vt):           Id = 0
    Linear (Vds < Vgs - Vt):     Id = k * ( (Vgs - Vt) * Vds - Vds^2 / 2 )
    Saturation (Vds >= Vgs - Vt): Id = (k / 2) * (Vgs - Vt)^2

where k = mu_n * Cox * (W / L), with Cox the oxide capacitance per unit area and W/L the channel width-to-length ratio. (Note that "saturation" means something different for MOSFETs than for BJTs: here it is the current-source region, used for amplification.) Modern short-channel devices deviate substantially from this model, but it captures the essentials: current set by gate voltage, and devices made stronger by making them wider (W) or shorter (L).

A p-channel MOSFET (PMOS) is the mirror image: n-type substrate, p-type source and drain, turned on by a gate voltage sufficiently below its source. Holes have lower mobility than electrons (Section 5.1), so PMOS transistors are weaker for the same size.

Early MOS integrated circuits used only PMOS (1960s), then NMOS (1970s), with resistor-like transistor loads. General Microelectronics introduced the first commercial MOS integrated circuit in 1964. MOS transistors were slower than bipolar ones at first, but they were much smaller and simpler to make, so far more could be put on a chip. The first microprocessors (Section 6.3) were PMOS and NMOS.

7. CMOS: complementary MOS

In 1963 Frank Wanlass and Chih-Tang Sah of Fairchild Semiconductor presented complementary MOS logic, which pairs NMOS and PMOS transistors so that, in either steady state, one of them is off. Wanlass filed a patent, granted in 1967. RCA introduced the CD4000 series of CMOS logic chips in 1968.

The CMOS inverter:

    Vdd
     |
    PMOS  (gate = input)
     |-------- output
    NMOS  (gate = input)
     |
    GND

  - Input low (0 V): PMOS on, NMOS off. Output connected to Vdd: high.
  - Input high (Vdd): PMOS off, NMOS on. Output connected to ground: low.

In either state there is no conducting path from Vdd to ground, so static power is (ideally) zero. Current flows only while the output is switching, to charge or discharge the load capacitance. Output levels swing fully from rail to rail, and noise margins are large (close to half the supply voltage in each direction).

CMOS NAND and NOR. For a 2-input NAND: two NMOS in series from output to ground (output is pulled low only if A AND B are both high), two PMOS in parallel from Vdd to output (output pulled high if A OR B is low). This is De Morgan's law (Section 1.1) made physical: the pull-down network computes AB, the pull-up network computes A' + B' = (AB)', and exactly one is conducting for any input combination. NOR swaps series and parallel. Compare the relay contacts of Section 2.1: series is AND, parallel is OR, exactly as Shannon showed in 1937.

Dynamic power. Each time a node of capacitance C switches from 0 to Vdd and back, energy C * Vdd^2 is drawn from the supply. For a chip with switching activity factor a (fraction of nodes switching per cycle) at clock frequency f:

    P_dynamic = a * C * Vdd^2 * f

This equation is the most important in modern chip design. It explains:

  - why lowering the supply voltage is so effective (power goes as Vdd squared); supply voltages fell from 5 V in the 1980s to around 1 V or less today;
  - why smaller transistors use less energy (smaller C);
  - why clock speeds stopped rising in the mid-2000s, when power density became unmanageable (Section 6.2), and the industry turned to parallelism: multicore CPUs and, for AI, massively parallel GPUs.

Static leakage. Real transistors are not perfect switches; as they shrank, subthreshold leakage and gate tunneling made static power significant again, which led to innovations like high-k gate dielectrics and FinFET and gate-all-around transistor structures (Section 6.2).

8. Why CMOS won

From the 1980s, CMOS displaced NMOS and bipolar logic for almost everything because:

  - near-zero static power allowed millions, then billions, of transistors per chip without melting;
  - full-swing outputs and wide noise margins make it robust;
  - its structure scales well as transistors shrink.

Bipolar logic held on in the fastest systems into the early 1990s, and bipolar transistors are still used in analog and RF circuits, and in power electronics (along with power MOSFETs and IGBTs) that you will use for motor drives.

9. Practical notes for mechatronics

  - Interfacing: a 3.3 V CMOS microcontroller output may not reach a 5 V TTL-compatible input's VIH, or may be damaged by 5 V inputs; check datasheet levels and use level shifters when needed.
  - Unused CMOS inputs must never float: a floating gate can sit near the threshold, turning both transistors partly on, wasting power and causing erratic behavior. Tie them high or low.
  - CMOS gates are sensitive to electrostatic discharge, because the thin gate oxide can be punctured by static; use ESD precautions.
  - Open-drain (or open-collector, in TTL) outputs allow wired-AND buses like I2C, using a shared pull-up resistor, a small revival of resistor pull-up logic.

10. Connection to AI

The energy per operation of CMOS logic, set by C * Vdd^2, ultimately limits how much computation an AI model can use for a given power budget. Training a large neural network today performs on the order of 10^23 to 10^26 arithmetic operations, and data centers are planned around their electricity supply. The historical decline in energy per switching event, from tubes to RTL to CMOS at nanometer scale, is what made modern deep learning physically possible, and its slowing is one of the central constraints on AI's future (Chapter 20).

11. Summary

  - Good logic gates need gain for level restoration, noise margins, fan-out, low delay and low power; the speed-power product measures energy per switch.
  - RTL (resistor-transistor) NOR gates were early and simple; the Apollo Guidance Computer used about 2,800 dual NOR-gate RTL chips in Block II.
  - DTL used diode logic with a transistor inverter; TTL (Buie, early 1960s; Sylvania 1963; TI 5400 in 1964 and 7400 in 1966) used multi-emitter inputs and totem-pole outputs and dominated for two decades.
  - ECL avoided saturation for maximum speed at high power.
  - The MOSFET (Atalla and Kahng, Bell Labs, 1959) switches by forming an inversion channel under an insulated gate; Id = (k/2)(Vgs - Vt)^2 in saturation.
  - CMOS (Wanlass and Sah, 1963) pairs NMOS and PMOS for near-zero static power; dynamic power P = a C Vdd^2 f governs chip design and the energy cost of AI.
